analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the broke savings-and-loan insurer, moves all deposit insurance to the FDIC, and sharply raises penalties for banking fraud.
analysis.headline: The sweeping savings-and-loan cleanup bill never left the Senate Banking Committee; after three days of hearings it was never reported or voted on before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the savings-and-loan collapse left the government's thrift deposit insurer broke, this bill would have abolished it and moved all deposit insurance to the FDIC. It would have created a new corporation to take over and sell off failed thrifts, financed with up to $50 billion in bonds plus scheduled Treasury payments. It also imposed much tougher accounting and capital rules on thrifts, made companies liable when their sibling institutions failed, and raised penalties for bank fraud from $1,000 a day to as much as $1 million a day. The bill never got past the Senate Banking Committee, which held hearings but never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Savers at savings and loans, whose insured deposits would have been protected by a financially strengthened FDIC system; taxpayers, who would gain a financed plan to contain the cost of failed thrifts rather than an open-ended liability; and honest bank employees, who would have gained whistleblower protection against being fired for reporting violations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Savers, depositors, and honest bank employees

how_it_helps.text: It would have moved all deposit insurance to the FDIC, replacing the insolvent FSLIC, and kept existing coverage in place automatically for savers at thrifts [S2][S3].

It would have raised daily civil penalties for violations of banking law from $1,000 to as much as $1,000,000 in cases of reckless disregard, doubled the statute of limitations for financial institution fraud to ten years, and extended criminal penalties to persons who violate removal orders at any federally insured institution [S2].

It would have protected whistleblowers, making it illegal for a federally insured institution to fire or discriminate against an employee who reports violations to regulators or the Justice Department [S2].

It would have ended capital forbearance — the practice of letting thinly capitalized thrifts keep operating — and required thrift capital standards no weaker than those applied to national banks [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The thrift industry, which would pay higher, permanently set insurance assessments (20.8 hundredths of a percent annually at first), lost its capital forbearance protections, and faced far larger penalties; commonly-controlled institutions, made liable for the FDIC's losses on a related failed institution; and taxpayers, through scheduled Treasury payments into the new savings-association insurance fund beginning in fiscal 1991.
analysis.who_pays_short: Thrift institutions and their holding companies

drawbacks.text: Taxpayers were put on the hook for the thrift cleanup: the Treasury was scheduled to pay between $2 billion and $8.8 billion a year into the savings association insurance fund from fiscal 1991 through 1999, on top of thrift industry assessments [S2].

While making healthy thrift operators liable for sister institutions' failures, the bill shielded bank-insured institutions from any liability for savings-association losses for five years, so one segment of the industry bore less of the cleanup cost [S2].
The bill allowed bank holding companies to acquire savings associations, letting larger banking companies absorb troubled thrifts rather than requiring owners to bear the losses themselves [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real emergency: the deposit insurance fund for savings and loans was failing, and letting it collapse would have hurt savers. The honest trade-off is that the cleanup was expensive — taxpayers were put on the hook for tens of billions of dollars in scheduled Treasury contributions, and the industry that caused the losses was not fully made whole by the cross-liability provision, which exempted bank-insured institutions from thrift losses for five years. It also opened the door for bank holding companies to buy thrifts, concentrating the industry further. Net: a costly but necessary stabilization, tilted in places toward the industry it was rescuing.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee: referred in February 1989, hearings in mid-March, then no further action for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 22, 1989, and referred the same day to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
The committee held hearings on March 15, 16, and 17, 1989 [S5].
No committee vote, floor vote, or further action is recorded before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1][S5].

The bill as written would have dissolved the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation, created the Resolution Trust Corporation to handle failed thrifts, and set up a Resolution Funding Corporation to sell up to $50 billion in bonds to finance the cleanup [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the pre-existing thrift regulatory structure and its weakened insurer were left standing a while longer, and no bank holding companies gained the new authority to acquire thrifts under this bill. The savings-and-loan cleanup eventually happened through other legislation later in 1989 rather than through this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The thrift industry's existing structure, briefly longer

for.name: Sen. Donald W. Riegle Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 22, 1989, and obtained Senate Banking Committee hearings on it in March 1989.

for.name: Sen. Jake Garn
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor of the bill.

for.name: Sens. Phil Gramm and Richard Shelby
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Held three days of hearings in March 1989 but never reported the bill to the full Senate, leaving it without a path to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was a Democrat and all three cosponsors were Republicans, giving it bipartisan sponsorship before it stalled in committee.

industries.note: The bill dismantled their insurer, ended capital forbearance, and imposed bank-level capital standards, but also put taxpayers' money behind cleaning up their failures and eventually funded their insurance fund through Treasury payments.

industries.industry: Commercial banks and bank holding companies
industries.note: The bill let bank holding companies acquire savings associations, opening the thrift industry to absorption by larger banking companies. It also shielded bank-insured institutions from liability for thrift defaults for five years.

industries.industry: Insiders at failed and failing thrifts
industries.note: Penalties for fraud, misapplication of funds, false statements, and bribery rose sharply, statutes of limitations doubled, and managers could be barred industry-wide from working at any insured institution.

industries.industry: Bond investors and the Resolution Funding Corporation structure
industries.note: The bill authorized up to $50 billion in tax-exempt bonds to finance the resolution of failed thrifts, creating a large new channel of government-backed borrowing administered by the Federal Home Loan Banks.
